utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We are Thursday, September the 18th, 2008. Good morning, Witness. Good morning to the accused, to Defence counsel, good morning to Mrs. West as well as Mr. Scott and the rest of the Prosecution team. And good morning to everybody else assisting us in these proceedings. One clarification from the Trial Chamber regarding the document which was challenged yesterday. According to the Defence, the document had not been admitted. The Trial Chamber checked if the document had been admitted or not, and it has been through the testimony of the expert witness Tomljanovich, which means that this document is actually admitted into evidence already. Thank you. This being said, I would like to give the floor to Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours and everyone in and around the courtroom. Thank you for that in regard to document, Your Honour, and I just want to clarify. I understand the exhibit number of that document to be 9689. The second thing I wanted to clarify this morning was the issue we left off yesterday which was a - thank you - statement of the former supervisor of the witness's. And we had a very poor copy of the original statement, and you also inquired whether we had a CLS translation. I went back to the office yesterday and found a much better copy of the original statement and the CLS translation. I will point out for counsel that just in -- just to be absolutely sure we had the CLSS translation looked at again yesterday to make sure that it was correct, and we've discovered one mistake on that and that would be in the English on the top of page 2 it says 27 June, when in fact that should be 27 May. I don't think that's a translation mistake as much as just a typo. So with that, Your Honour, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apologies. My apologies, Your Honours. Yesterday I intervened in relation to the document that was just mentioned, P 9689. I really must emphasize that it has not been exhibited. Yesterday the registrar confirmed as much. Let me only say that it was not my intention to do this deliberately. I double-checked it. We can check it again. It is not in e-court as an exhibit. The registrar confirmed so, and we will try and see where the error was why we didn't have that information. Thank you, and I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Puljic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yesterday we left off and we were talking about the statement of Mr. Jahic your former supervisor; do you remember talking about that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Just to go back to that, I had read a portion of it that was in the very first paragraph. I'm not going to re-read the whole paragraph, but I'll go to the part in which you had a comment. Mr. Jahic had stated that he noticed that the documents had been printed before the Serb-Chetnik army's aggression against the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and they had been printed in the Grude printing house in December 1991 and -- excuse me, in January and February 1992. Now, yesterday you indicated that not to be true; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true because at the time there did not exist any printing works in Grude. However, one did exist in Mostar where documents were printed, and all the documents that were printed at the time were printed at that particular company, and we have them listed here in reference to different time-periods. Only Mostar had a printing works in 1991/1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So in December 1991 there were -- there was an operating printing company in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So there was the ability as early as December to have documents printed; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That printing house was in the close proximity of the front line. It did not operate. Before the start of the war, it was closely controlled by the authorities and this type of documents could not be printed, if that's what you're referring to, to the state-owned printing house. In other words, before the war there was just this one printing house, one company, in Herzegovina and that was the one in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And at the time you did not live in Grude; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't, but it's a small town and I passed through it every day on -- one passes through it every day on the way to Split. I didn't live in Grude, but I know as much.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to look at another individual who was on the Crisis Staff and that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, you had just mentioned that the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats started in May 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: During this whole time you lived in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you live in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I lived in my home in West Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And how long had you been living in that home?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I started building my house four to five years before the war, and I moved into the house a half a year before the Serb aggression. In other words, I had been living in that home half a year before this -- for half a year before the Serb aggression, and then since my house was shelled, I lived in my father's house for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When did you move to your father's house?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I moved there in early May or late April 1992. I spent there several months until I was able to repair my house that was damaged in the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And when did you go back to your own home in West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both homes are in West Mostar, and I went back to my house some three to four months later; in other words, it could have been July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And did you remain in that home throughout the HVO-Muslim war?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, I'm just going to -- Mr. Puljic, we're going to back up a little bit. You -- is it fair to say that as the special-purpose council, which then became the HVO government, took control of Mostar you had testified that that took a period of time there was still intervention and help from the Sarajevo government?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, I object to the form of the question. I understand what counsel wishes to do, but look at the question, look at the question, Your Honours. The special-purpose council was as we saw from the documents had six days from the time that it was entrusted without anybody's notice to take over the entire civilian government, six days later a civilian government was formed. So when you look at that question, it really does beg another question: Why are we trying to force these sorts of facts into a question which have not been established. Now, she can rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, you keep objecting. We're wasting a lot of time because of such objections. When a lawyer asks a question, even if the lawyer [as interpreted] is badly formulated, Judges do realize what's happening, we're not stupid, we understand the question, and we understand the limitations of the questions. We listen to the answer provided by the witness and of course the answer depends on the question asked, and depending on what the answer is then we'll give it value or no value at all. So if the question is badly formulated -- well, the lawyer asking the question has a risk, you know, the risk being that no probative value or hardly any is going to be given to the answer provided. This is an international Tribunal with competent, able Judges; Judges who are able to understand a badly formulated question and to understand an answer. Fine. Fine. Your objection has been recorded in the transcript, but this is a waste of time. Please continue, and please try to take into account what Mr. Karnavas has said in order to avoid permanent objections.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, is it fair to say that there was still intervention and help from the Sarajevo government?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are two inaccurate facts in that question. First you said that the special-purpose council had taken over the role of the civilian authority; this is something that never happened. Second, no sort of contact was possible at the time with Sarajevo, that is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, let's look at 1D 01619.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: What binder?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. President. It's 1D 01619. It's the first binder, Mr. President -- my apologies, Mr. President, I'm told it's the second binder, but nonetheless it's on the screen, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, this is a document that is dated on the second page of the English 21 May 1992 in Sarajevo, and this is a document that is entitled: Decision on loans to municipalities from permanent reserve funds of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and under Article 1 it says: "Loans from permanent reserve funds are hereby granted to municipalities as follows in dinars ..." And if you go down to number 31 do you see Mostar? It says 50 million.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it all, including number 31.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And as a member of government at the time, local government at the time, were you aware of these loans?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The money never reached Mostar to my knowledge, at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should have known had they -- had the funds been transferred.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to look at 1D 02684, it should be right in the same binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: 2684, it's also on the screen in front of you. And this is a letter on a Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina letterhead and it's to the Croatian Defence Council in Mostar, and it's regarding the HVO's request for guarantees for an international loan. Now, when is -- do you see the date on this?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 17th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Right. And this is well -- well after the war began; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're talking about a war beginning. At that point the conflict between the Serbs and the events in Mostar had ceased to exist. I mean, that needs to be distinguished. So -- I mean, I see the way the question is phrased, as if it's an ongoing war. At that point normalcy has returned to some point in Mostar; there lies the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'll rephrase my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: October 17th, 1992, as counsel has indicated, did normalcy return to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the shelling was still going on, but the situation was more or less normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And at this time you see the first small paragraph or sentence says: "We have received your request," and it gives a number, "of 5 October of this year referring to giving guarantees for an international loan of US $5 million ..." Would you agree with me that at least during this time this shows an interaction between Mostar and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If somebody carried a letter through the tunnel or -- or say through UNPROFOR or carried a letter into Sarajevo or out of Sarajevo, I still don't consider that to be a proper contact.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I'm going to direct your attention to testimony given to this Chamber by Zoran Perkovic and this is testimony from September 1st of this month, so just recent testimony, and it's page of the transcript it's 31689 and it's lines 15 to 22 and in it Perkovic says that: "Throughout the war while the Croatian community and later the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna were in existence, there was contact between the republican institutions in Sarajevo and the people who sat in institutions of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I personally was in contact with these people several times, even at the time when the Croat-Muslim/Croat-Bosniak conflict was at its highest level ..." So, Mr. Puljic, do I understand that although other people -- in this case, excuse me, Mr. Perkovic had contact with Sarajevo, you personally did not have any?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any contacts with Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But that does not preclude the possibility of other people having contact; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time every person in Sarajevo wanted to have some kind of a task to establish some kind of a contact with someone outside and to flee from Sarajevo in that way and save their lives. I would not be surprised if you were to find some 50 situations of people trying to establish contact.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to talk to you now about the issue of water, and you had testified I think it was the day before yesterday and talked about it yesterday as well about the sources of water-supply to West and East Mostar. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And let me summarize it and just tell me if this is correct or if I have it wrong. The water originated at a particular source. It passed through the settlement of Rastane, and as it passed you testified along the length of exposed fire to Muslim troops. It came through West Mostar and the only way to get it into East Mostar was over the bridges; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you testified that the ABiH fired on the people who tried to repair the lines for strategy purposes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, that's a mis-characterization of the testimony, Your Honour. I believe there was a question from the Bench which asked whether it was strategic or not, and the gentleman was quite modest in his answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas is correct, it was a question from the Bench that mentioned strategy.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But was your answer to that question yes?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer was yes, I can confirm that the employees of the public enterprise were fired at.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, if the water -- in order for people in East Mostar to get water, it had -- the water first had to go through West Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In order for East Mostar to receive water, it first, the water, went through West Mostar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, through West Mostar and across the bridges.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so if those pipelines were fired at resulting in West Mostar not receiving any water, it would also result in East Mostar not receiving any water; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, East Mostar had no water already, so you cannot engage in assumptions like that. There was no water in East Mostar already because there were no bridges.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'd like to look at P 02611 and this was a handout yesterday morning, and that's P 02611. It's also on the screen in front of you. This is a letter dated June 2nd, 1993; it's from Arif Pasalic and the letterhead is the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now, in it, in the very first page, which is the letter he talks about the problem of water on the left bank and the second paragraph, and I'll read this: "We are also informing you that we are giving you all guarantees from our part that works in the area of responsibility under the control of the BH Army will be carried out without any interruption, and we will give necessary protection during the execution of works and also necessary manpower ..." Now, if you go to the attachment which will be the second page, I believe, he's describing the situation with water in East Mostar. In the first paragraph he says that there are 25.000 inhabitants on the left bank and the whole area has not been supplied by sanitary water since the beginning -- excuse me, since the moment of destruction of the city bridges, which you've also confirmed for us. The second paragraph indicates: "For the moment being, the complete left bank is supplied by water through 4 temporary crossings of plastic pipes having diameters of 2 inches and 1 and a quarter inches ..." At the bottom of that he writes: "Logically, because of shortage of water the complete sewage system is not in function at all on the left bank of the river. We stress that there are enough sufficient capacities of water sources for supply of the whole area of the city of Mostar." If you go to the next page, which will be the third page in English, here he offers a solution, and it has three points in it. I'll read this and ask you some questions about it. He says: "For the solution of the key problem of the left bank, we are suggesting the following schedule of activities ..." It says: "Finishing of activities with THW-Germany for construction of the transport water pipeline over the bridge having a diameter for 300 millimetres ... the second part is preparing of a transfer network for rinsing and disinfecting, the third part is electronic machine workshop shall also be included." At the very bottom, the last sentence he says: "We are also stressing that inhabitants of the left bank are ready to hear extraordinary efforts and give help to the whole action including all the structure of civilian protection and the BH Army." Mr. Puljic, my question for you, at this time this is June 1993, it appears that this letter suggests that people in East Mostar were in dire need of that water; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a fact; however, there is another thing that this letter says to me: In order to get water you first have to building a waterworks.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But does it -- go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This letter, if you were to add up the number of letters, words, and sentences, 99 per cent of it pertains to how you can get water and the way you can get water is by building a waterworks.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so when you say waterworks, under number 1 on the page in front of you it says: "Finishing of activities with THW-Germany for construction of transport water pipeline ..." Is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I was not aware of these activities of the THW in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. But you'll agree with me that this letter indicates that the BH army was willing to even help to ensure that the water ultimately ended up in East Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that this letter indicates that the BH army, the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, was willing to even help ensure that the water ultimately ended up in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you've put a question and you've already given an answer yourself by putting the question that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so my question is: Do you agree --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army is just providing a solution here as to how it could be done.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is to say they are making a proposal to build a waterworks.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I now am going to read some testimony that was taken by this Court on May 14th, 2007, and it's -- it was Witness BC, and I'm reading from page of the transcript 18331 and then I will ask you a question about this. The question is: "Q. Can you tell us just a little bit about the situation regarding water as of this point, which is June of 1993?" And the answer from Witness BC is: "The situation at that stage was that there were very, very limited -- we were told two small pipes that provided water to the east -- east part of the city, so the majority of the inhabitants there would have been either going to those pipes and been subject to incoming sniper fire from the west side, or, and this is what the majority of the people did, going to the Neretva River to get their water, which is also very dangerous thing to do because of sniper fire." And the next question is: "THW, what is THW?" And the answer is: "It's a German government organization, humanitarian organization, that very often is involved in water and sanitation projects and humanitarian crises." And the following question: "And what were they doing down in Mostar in respect to the water?" The answer: "They had an engineer down there who was trying to undertake a project to restore in a limited fashion a water-supply from the western part of the city to the eastern part of the city." Now, moving to page 18332, line 4: "Q. Do you know whether he succeeded in providing water to the east side at the time? "A. He didn't. Unfortunately, he did not succeed. He spent his days in Mostar negotiating with the Bosnian Croat authorities responsible for the water-supply system in the west side of the city to get permission to undertake this repair project. He needed their permission to do that, and unfortunately he was very, very frustrated and ultimately gave up for lack of permission for the Bosnian Croat authorities to undertake that project." Mr. Puljic, were you aware that this was going on at the time in June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to I object to the form of the question. That assumes that the gentleman is accurately describing the events. It should be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. West has just read what Witness BC said. It's quite interesting to find out what this witness here would think of it. He can say that it's true, it's false -- I mean, that's what confrontation is all about after all. You confront one declaration with another and with the statements of another. Maybe BC told the truth, maybe he was a bit evasive. It's good to confront this witness with what the other witness said. What do you say of this, please, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time that is described in this statement, I was director of the public enterprise for the construction and reconstruction of Mostar. It had almost stopped functioning because of the situation that the city was facing, that is to say only a few of us came to work. I was compelled to spend most of my time at home. I have no knowledge from that time as to what happened at the negotiations, and I don't have any knowledge as to what the situation was on the left bank. When speaking of waterworks, I would kindly ask that questions pertaining to waterworks be reduced to the level of my knowledge. I, as a town planner, know how the waterworks functioned in an infrastructural sense and in a town planning sense; and I was answering questions along those lines yesterday, and I thought that that would be the situation today. At any rate, at that point in time I had no knowledge of what the situation was on the left bank or what the situation was in terms of the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two short questions for you, and I believe that they will sum up the situation. You lived in West Mostar, you said so. I have a simple question for you. Throughout all this time were there any difficulties with the water-supply in West Mostar, in your everyday life to wash or clean or drink?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All that time there were problems in terms of water-supply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you ever have to go without drinking because there was no water?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. First of all, the pressure was not good throughout and sometimes there was no water all together. Then we who live a bit higher up would go to the houses that are lower down and perhaps there could be water in those houses but then sometimes there wasn't any water there either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Secondly, to your knowledge in East Mostar did you have any information regarding the water-supply that would state that there were problems with the water-supply?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that they did have problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, I'm looking at a sentence here you have said which I quote: "I have no knowledge from that time as to what happened at the negotiations, and I don't have any knowledge as to what the situation was on the left bank." Did your mandate have a limitation to West Mostar at that time? Did you consider your task to be limited to the western part of the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not think that my work was limited to the west part of town only. It had to do with the entire city. However, at that moment the public enterprise for the reconstruction and construction of Mostar, in view of the fact that there was a war going on, in view of the fact that the building was 100 metres away from the boulevard, it simply couldn't function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, you would agree with me in April -- April through June of 1992 Mostar was -- suffered under shelling from the Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And the Serb shelling was voluminous, you would agree that it was a difficult time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Would you also agree that in 1993, post-May 1993, particularly the end of 1993 into the beginning of 1994 that the shelling going into East Mostar was also quite voluminous?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military experts should answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you as a resident of West Mostar, a resident of a fairly small city, whether you could observe first-hand the shelling of the city.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you are putting questions to me which require subjective rather than objective answers. You know, if a shell is flying at you then it has to do with a subjective thing. I have no way of knowing. I do not have this information. You have to have military experts -- you have to ask military experts what the word "intensive" means terminologically. That is to say I cannot answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Let's not beat around the bush. You live in West Mostar, you're not challenging this, and there's shelling going on flying into East and West Mostar, and this is the question you must answer: Did you know whether East Mostar was shelled? You're answering: No, I had no idea, I didn't know anything. Or you answer: Yes, I heard about it or I heard some shelling. But now you're telling us that we should ask an expert to answer this question. We don't want an answer from an expert. We would like to know whether when you lived in West Mostar you could hear the shelling on East Mostar and were aware of that East Mostar was being shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with all due respect you're mis-characterizing the witness's testimony. The issue came down to intensity not whether he saw or not, and I think that's where he's saying on the issue of intensity it's subjective. He never said that he didn't see anything. So perhaps if the question can be rephrased in a manner which may not make -- the gentleman answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, unless I'm mistaken I didn't feel that you were asking a question about the intensity of the shelling; you were asking a question to know whether East Mostar had been shelled. Was the question on the intensity of the shelling or the actual shelling itself?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The term I used, Your Honour, was voluminous, which I think is different from intensity. To avoid that entirely if we can back up and ask the question you asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, while living in West Mostar, did you have an opportunity to make observations, whether that being seeing things or hearing things, regarding the shelling in the whole city? Let's start there, East Mostar and West Mostar.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard shells falling on Eastern Mostar but also I heard firing at the western part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: At the time did it appear to you - and the time-frame I'm talking about is late 1993/early 1994 - did it appear to you that East Mostar was receiving more shelling than West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in my view - unless I'm mistaken perhaps - again this opens a completely new topic. I do not recall that so far in such situations the Trial Chamber gave general permission to the Prosecutor to bring up topics that had not been raised during the examination-in-chief. So far on several occasions, and I think that this was your explicit ruling, on several occasions you did allow the Prosecution to broach subjects that had not been broached during the direct examination, but these were specific approvals in specific cases. Now the Prosecutor is going into subjects that were not dealt with during the examination-in-chief, they are not even referring to Rule 90(H), they are not even asking for permission to do that. So now does the Prosecution believe that they have your general approval that they can raise new subjects whenever they feel it is necessary? In the meantime this can harm us. Give us the right to cross-examine because the Prosecution case has been closed. They could have proven --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Yesterday when Mr. Karnavas asked questions, the witness spontaneously talked about the shelling and the intensity of the shelling; he mentioned that yesterday. So the Prosecutor is now dealing with the subject --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may, I've been following this carefully. Praljak too, yes, that's right, that's right, Judge Trechsel, Mr. Praljak too, but we're talking about two completely different events: Questions put by Mr. Karnavas and the questions put by General Praljak had to do with 1992, the time when the JNA and the Serbs were shelling and bombing Mostar. Now my colleague is speaking of 1993 and 1994, different parties, a different war altogether, a different story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me consult with my fellow Judges to see if we allow Madam West to deal with this now topic?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I be heard first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber believes that in the interests of justice the witness should be asked questions on shelling, whatever period is considered. So you have the floor, Mrs. West.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honour, two points. I am respectful of your ruling, but I wish to state for the transcript that in my view this ruling is not in accordance with the law. We have filed a motion and you will render your decision. However, our basic viewpoint is that the Prosecution case is over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's on the transcript. But you can go on now, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We'll go to backing to my question and the question at line 14 is: At the time did it appear to you, the time-frame being late 1993/early 1994, did it appear that East Mostar was receiving more shelling than West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When there is shelling you hear the sound of the shell being fired, the shell flying through the air, and then the shell blasting or impacting. When a shell is fired then every normal person covers one's ears and ducks one's head, and it doesn't even cross his mind to busy himself or herself with counting shells.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, I'm going to show you a report to see if this may help you give us an answer as to shelling at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But may we go into closed session -- private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, is it fair to say that the city of Mostar on the whole suffered more damage under the HVO in 1993 and 1994 than it did under the Serb siege from April to June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In answer to your question, I think that there are precise indicators and figures, but they need to be retrieved. In the first war, during the Serb aggression, the town was absolutely destroyed as testified by the book entitled: "Urbicide," and as indicated by all the figures, numbers drawn up by the commissions for the assessment of damage which were made up of professionals and were multi-ethnic and worked under uniform methodology. It was according to the same methodology that the assessment of damage was done after the second conflict, and this is something that can be ascertained.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But you live --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first part of the war, shelling was the dominant feature; as for the second, this is something you were able to see when the war ended and when one took a walk around the town, you could see that all the buildings were bullet-riddled. So after the first war you would be able to see buildings damaged or destroyed by shells; after the second part of the war, you were able to see bullet-riddled facades of the buildings. Therefore, I can confirm here that major destruction in the town was inflicted in the first part of the war, during the Serb aggression. There are indicators testifying to that, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay, but you've not answered my question which has to do with damage. In --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I? I didn't wish to intervene before and my colleague is going back to the question. Look at the question more closely, please. The question is pure speculation. This is an assessment on the part of the Prosecution that damage was greater in one period than in the other, so lege artis my learned friend had to lay a foundation for the statement contained in her question, though of course I don't know of any direct evidence that could confirm what she said. But this is the thesis in the indictment. So in accordance with Rule 90(H), she should have said, Witness, I put it to you that on the basis of this and that damage inflicted in 1993 was heavier than in 1992. Now that she received an answer that was not to the expectation of the Prosecution, she is trying to go back to the same question through the backdoor and that's contrary to the rules governing cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, if I understood that through your question you were asking to -- you were asking the witness to talk about damage. He answered and said that according to him during the Serb aggression the damage -- the shelling damage was heavier than what he noticed on buildings after the other aggression because -- after the other war because there was the walls were bullet-riddled. That's all he answered, and that's not enough for you? You want more?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I do respectfully, Mr. President. I think particularly this witness, having been the author or the overseer of a book about damage after the Serb siege and an architect who lives in the area, he should be able to give a far more thorough answer regarding damage in the city. So I am going to ask him again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I looked at your book very carefully, of course. Your book is extremely interesting with photographs, and it's an interesting read. Now, why didn't you have -- why didn't you write the same book but for the period after the Serb aggression, 1993 to 1994? Maybe you didn't have enough time, maybe you plan on doing this, very well. But it would have been interesting to take a building, for example, a given building, photograph that building as you did so that we could see the damage inflicted during the Serb aggression and then take a new picture of that building to show that after 1993/1994 either the building had not been further damaged or had been further damaged or had been repaired. Did you undertake this kind of work, comparison work, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the end of the second conflict in Mostar, European administration was set up in Mostar; in other words, the town was governed by the European administration headed by Mr. Hans Koschnik. The European administration had all the information dating from the first war since we had it collected and stored, and primarily this was part of the effort that I took part in that was carried out in Mostar. After the second part of the conflict an assessment was made of war damage; however, I did not personally take part in making that assessment, other departments were involved in that. I can only give you an impression that of an engineer strolling the town, and I can tell you that the damage in the two periods is incomparable; in other words, the damage inflicted in the second part of the conflict was drastically less than in the first. Another problem of methodological nature comes into play here as well. You have to be able to objectively assess the damage. After the second war, the emotions were so strong that it was almost impossible to do or it was very difficult to. After the first war, as you could see in the book called Urbicide there were buildings that were destroyed regardless of who destroyed them. In Urbicide you can see the Serb Orthodox church that was destroyed, because at the time we both wanted and were able to be objective. After the second conflict I think it was the emotions that barred any sort of objective analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, would that, what you have just told us, and very understandable, big emotions, could that also have influenced your finding that the damages were drastically less than in the first war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hardly. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, on direct testimony you spoke about a conference that you had attended, it was in April of 1993, where you presented a paper as well. It was in Neum and I think it was under the auspices of the University of Mostar, and I'd like to look at that paper, it's 1D 02706. That's binder 2. Thank you. In front of you -- this is the paper you wrote for that conference; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So in the very first paragraph you wrote about Urbicide. And you wrote: "In history, there have been rare examples of 'urbicide' a systematic and planned destruction of a town. We understand this term to mean the destruction of a town which is the goal, not a consequence, of war operations." And the last sentence you write: "Simply, by destroying a city, the greatest product of civilization, the intention was to stop the civilizational progress of a whole nation and wipe out its roots and its greatest material and cultural achievements accumulated for generations." Now, this conference that you attended was this also attended by other colleagues in the same business who also wrote papers like this?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this paper would have come on the heels of your book: "Mostar 1992," right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these are two different papers. The 1992 Urbicide book contained one set of articles and this one contains a different set.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. So "Mostar 1992," you had testified came at the end of 1992 and it went on exhibition; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I believe you testified Split, Zagreb, and then went to the UNESCO centre in Paris?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Ljubljana.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also testified that there was also a film that was involved?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, there are a number of articles in "Mostar 1992," but you wrote a couple of them but other people wrote the rest; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But nonetheless you organized it and you oversaw the whole project; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Would you consider this to be a comprehensive and accurate assessment of war damage post-Serb siege?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first objective and accurate assessment. It was followed by only one such accurate assessment, and to my knowledge the data contained therein do not differ much because they were professionals of different nationalities who had the expertise and who did go from home to home to collect information. But to go back to this, yes, the information contained here is objective and accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And this -- you've just said that it was followed by only one other such accurate assessment. Are you referring to another book about the Serb siege?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to the official paper made by the official commissions which had specific forms and I believe that we looked at them the first or the second day that listed the methodology according to which war damage was to be assessed. The only difference is that their job was done in a bit more detail than the one by the engineers of the public enterprise for the construction and reconstruction of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, did your role of overseeing this book include making decisions regarding what articles to include in the book and which photos to include in the book?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part of the job was done collectively. I did not, and that's a fact, correct or look to correct a single page, a single word or sentence in that book without consulting others first. Some of them I even didn't manage to read through all the way before they were sent to be printed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we can look at the book and it's 3D 00785.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, Your Honour, refer to only one sentence in this article, a single sentence. At the time I was writing this, I wasn't aware of this but there is one sentence which is absolutely consistent with my knowledge today, the destruction of a town can be urbicide, it can be the goal, but it can also be the consequence. In the first war we had urbicide, whereas the destruction of this town in the second war was a consequence of the war. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification for the record, it would appear that on page 36, and I'm trying to -- line 21, the gentleman indicated that he had not made a single correction to a single page, single word, or sentence in that book, but as I am told, he did not say "without consulting others first," in other words, you know, full stop as opposed to he did make some corrections but he consulted others first. So perhaps that can be clarified, the gentleman can be given an opportunity to clarify that part of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, you heard comments by counsel. When you made decisions regarding this book, maybe made corrections, did you consult first with others on your team before you made those corrections?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I oversaw the entire exercise, but the book is a collective product. This means the following: You could see that articles were authored by two or three individuals. Simply, because of the time, we didn't even have time to consult with each other or to comment on the articles. Almost -- it almost happened so that we would forward for printing raw material without having time to work on it. While working on the book, I never consulted with anyone else other than the individuals mentioned in the book, and it was in the technical sense, to make the book better. I personally didn't correct a single article. We tried to place them in a certain order. I chose the topics and the people who would be covering various topics, and when the time came four or five of us sat down and physically put it all together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just before the break I have one small question. I was looking at this paper called "Urbicide," and I was looking at the table on page 2, it's quite striking. You drew up a summary chart, hotels, municipality buildings, cultural buildings, department stores, bridges, and religious structures, churches. The mosques are not included. But what's really interested here in this table is that you're giving the figures before the war, for example, you have nine hotels before the war, and then you give the distribution between those that are damaged, destroyed, or intact. We note that hardly any buildings stayed intact. And then you draw up the percentage of destruction, 100 per cent of hotels were destroyed, 100 per cent of municipal buildings were destroyed, 83 per cent of cultural buildings were destroyed, all department stores were 100 per cent destroyed, 92 per cent of the bridges were destroyed, and 91 per cent of the churches were destroyed. So it seems that almost everything was destroyed. So what -- starting from that you really wonder what could be -- what could be further destroyed. It's -- it's really striking. It looks like the entire city was in ruins. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. Look at the photographs and everything will be clear to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I have one more question before we break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In relation to this table you have religious structures of the Catholic church but you don't include mosques, why don't you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably it's an error.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's break for 20 minutes. My fellow Judge has something to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I just want for the record to declare that unfortunately I will not be able to sit after the break today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in session. Ms. West, Mr. Registrar told me you'd used two hours and 44 minutes. So in theory you have one hour and 15 minutes left. So if there aren't too many objections, we could complete your cross-examination before the second break. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, I'd like to now talk about your book.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Your Honour, I should really give an explanation with regard to the last answer I gave before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was why there were no mosques in that table. We participated in this gathering as individuals but also as the representatives of the institutions that we came from originally. So we from the public enterprise for reconstruction and construction had agreed to go with three scientific papers. I was supposed to speak of the future development of town and the paper was written in that sense. In the second paper the group that dealt with the protection of cultural heritage was supposed to deal with that subject. All cultural monuments had been dealt with within that topic and the reconstruction of mosques and Islamic monuments was the particular focus of that group. In the third group were engineers who presented their methods of reconstructing bridges on the Neretva River. What I'm saying is that the subject of mosques was dealt with in another paper by this group of people who also spoke there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, we're going to go directly to your book and I'm going to show you plate 43. We're going to put this on the ELMO because I think the quality is going to be better and this is the new Orthodox church or Serbian Orthodox cathedral of Holy Trinity church in Mostar. Now, this is the only photo in your book of this particular Orthodox church and it's an after photo. Do you recognise that photo?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In the book, in the beginning where the articles are placed, there is some mention of this and it's page 39 of the English, page 21 of the B/C/S, and it says that: "The new Orthodox church was set on fire in the final operations while the enemy was retreating from Mostar." And then it says: "And sometime later the church was destroyed by the self-willed act of unknown perpetrators." Do you remember when this church was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In fact this was destroyed later on in June after the JNA had already pulled out of Mostar. Does that help you remember the exact date?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that it took place after the JNA had pulled out.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And you agree that in order to have an explosion like this or the result of this destruction, a large amount of explosives would have been used?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And also would you agree with me that it would be unlikely that the Serbs would have exploded their own Orthodox church --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation. Obviously my learned colleague has no clue of what was happening in that war, and I can point to countless of examples including in Sarajevo. That totally calls for speculation. I'm shocked that an attorney of her calibre would even ask a question of such nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have no idea as to whom may have been at the origin of the damage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One morning when I went to work I saw this silhouette of the city, and I realized that the Orthodox church was no longer there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, I'm going to move on to the old Orthodox church. What you have in front of you is the new Orthodox church, now we're going to move to the old Orthodox church. You'll agree with me that there's no photo of that church in your book; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a lot of photographs are not in my book, or rather, many damaged facilities and not all the churches are there, not all the mosques are there. But we wanted to paint a picture of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But nonetheless your book does mention the old Orthodox church and this is page 39 of the English and page 21 of the B/C/S and it says: "The structure suffered no damage ..." So indeed post-Serb siege the old Orthodox church actually was not damaged; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The old Orthodox church is behind the new Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And it suffered no damage during the Serb siege?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Couldn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, turn to page 39 of your book which is right in front of you.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Page 39 of the book in front of you and it's page 21 of the English. And this is an article that recounts the damage to a number of the Orthodox churches, and you'll agree with me that your group reported that this church suffered no damage post-Serb siege.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to read this in order to be able to give you an answer. Where is this? What?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We're just going to move on. You're familiar with the church, though, nonetheless; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Now, isn't it true that it was ultimately blown up during the night on January 14th and 15th of 1993?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the old church or the new church?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm talking about the old church and there's a picture of it -- old picture of it right in front of you on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to show you another photo of this church and this is a photo that was taken in the spring of 1994. And this is P 10607, and for the record the book we showed earlier with the before picture -- excuse me, this is P 10607, the last numbers being 1756. This is a photo, do you recognise, of the old Orthodox church post-Croat/Muslim war?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the church but this church could never be seen from town, that is to say that it was behind the new Orthodox church. And even when the new Orthodox church was destroyed you couldn't see this one because of the ruins when viewed from town. I never went to this locality specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So are you telling me that you've never seen this church?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Objection. That's not what he's indicated. And I'm again -- I call upon my colleague to kindly resort -- or stop resorting to these sorts of tactics. Listen to what the gentleman indicated, you could not see it from that location, not that he never saw it. There is a big distinction. I don't see why we need to resort to these sorts of sleazy tactics.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness can answer the question and if the answer to that question is no, he can give it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. The question has to be fair. She is twisting what he said. She -- the question assumes facts that are not in evidence and it's a sleazy tactic and I'm calling my counsel on it -- the Prosecution on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may, one word. I -- [Interpretation] I'm confused. I don't see the relevance of this question. I've checked the indictment once again. There are no charges in the indictment that involve the destruction of Orthodox churches. I don't see what the relevance is. I know that the Prosecutor is entitled to her own four hours, but it doesn't give her the right to put any kind of question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, does your question go to show something in the indictment? Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question goes to this gentleman's credibility. He indicated that the second war, 1993/1994, the city of Mostar suffered much less damage. The photo in front of him was taken in May 1994. That is a Serb Orthodox church and not one of the churches -- the indictment does not make it irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how do we know that the Muslims didn't blow it up?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That is an issue for re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How do we know -- no, the whole point is relevancy. That's the point, it goes to relevancy and this is Trial Advocacy 101; it has nothing to do with post or pre. If she can connect that this damage was actually done by the Croats, I can see the line of questioning. But how does one photograph of one church in one location support her thesis and how is it relevant to the indictment? Now, if she can connect the dots on that I'll sit down; but until then, I'll keep objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, for relevance purposes I asked the question, Mr. Kovacic raised the issue, what is the relevance of this question with regards to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, the relevance is the damage that was caused during the 1993/1994 war. Now, although the indictment lists very particular things, it doesn't mean that there was damage otherwise. And this particular witness has offered testimony to the Trial Chamber that in 1994 the damage was much less. This is an example of how that is not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect [Interpretation] Maybe my English is not good enough. I haven't heard the interpretation, but this is what my colleague said [In English] In particular things it does not mean that there was damage otherwise. [Interpretation] Does that mean that we have to see whether there are any elements that the Prosecutor has that are not in the indictment? Something is either in the indictment or not, something is relevant and therefore -- or perhaps irrelevant, but I cannot agree that say something may have happened although it's not in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know the Defence was going to object on this. I don't have the indictment before me, but if I remember well in the indictment I believe we're talking about mass-scale destruction. There are lists of religious buildings which were destroyed, but this list is not comprehensive. There are other examples - correct me if I'm wrong, Ms. West - but if I understood correctly, your question goes to show that there has been mass-scale destructions; and that's why you're showing this picture to the witness. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You may not fully grasp those discussions, witness, but the fundamental issue that is of interest to the Chamber is who did it, who destroyed those religious buildings. It seems you have no idea as to whom did it; that's what you said earlier on. So if you're shown various pictures I guess we'll get the same answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who did this or when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. He's already said that he didn't know, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to move on -- back to your book and this is a mosque that was mentioned earlier, and it's plate 16 of your book. This is the Karadjoz Mehmet Bey Mosque. It was mentioned yesterday by Ms. Nozica, it's in the indictment, and if you look on the screen in front of you, you'll see the photo. Do you recognise that mosque?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this was one of Mostar's most notable Ottoman-era buildings and it was its principal mosque; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the principles of Ottoman architecture, there is no main mosque in a town. All mosques are equal. So this same concept of urban form and urban content is not like it is in the West. In the West you have a square, a cathedral, a town hall, but in an eastern town all mosques are equal. Among other things, we should make a distinction. There are some mosques that belong to the carsija and the other ones that belong to the Mahalas, the residential areas. This is the mosques of one of the Mahalas, and it is one of the Mostar mosques that are related to a particular neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. This mosque is also listed with the register of historic monuments; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to show you another photo of the mosque, and this was taken in May of 1994. You agree with me by May of 1994 the mosque has suffered more damage?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Well, the angle is not the same. The photographs were taken from different angles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the first picture again, please. Madam Usher, could you please put back on the ELMO the first picture. Put them together if possible, one next to the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Puljic -- excuse me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, you see the photos in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You'll agree with me that the photo on the left it appears that a large chunk of the main dome is destroyed?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have to agree with you?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, no, you tell me if --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You always ask me: Will you agree with me or you will agree with me. The differences in terms of destruction, that is a question for expertise. The witness is not an expert, but I can answer as an engineer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, who has knowledge in photography it seems. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if a person knows this mosque and if a person knows where the dome and where the minaret are, it is obvious that the first photograph was taken from a different side than the one on the right-hand side, so it's two different angles. The first one is facing the east, the Serb side; and the other one is facing the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Ms. West, the two pictures were taken from different angles. It may be or not, I'm not saying that it's a certain fact, but it may be that the destruction seen on the left side also exists on the right-hand picture but because of the angle you can't see it. Technically speaking, I'm not saying it's not possible. Witness, as an architect, what can you say? The Prosecution is asking you if on the left side picture there are indications of further destruction as compared to the picture on the right, irregardless of the angle. What can you say? Can you confirm? Do you have reservations? Are you challenging the Prosecution's position? What do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Prosecutor said that these two photographs were taken at two different points in time and that the year had elapsed in the meantime, for instance. I just wish to state that the mosque and its main dome and the three smaller domes in front were made of stone and that the front eaves were made of wood. I cannot assess the damage. I can see that the wooden porch has caved in. Now, whether that happened because of the effects of the first shelling or perhaps some new shelling, I really cannot say. This is a question for expertise and a more serious viewing of the problem and this is something that should be worked on more seriously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But on the dome on the left side picture there's been an impact because there's a hole. Can you see the dome? There's a huge hole there on the picture on the left. What's your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, whether it's due to caving in or shelling is something that would have to be established by construction experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, now I'm going to show you another mosque that was mentioned yesterday by Ms. Nozica, it's plate 18 of the book, it's the Nesuh Aga V-A-C-J-A-K-O-V-I-C Mosque. Do you see that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nasu Aga Vucjakovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And that mosque did suffer some damage from the Serb siege; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard to say on the basis of a sing photograph, but I do see that the minaret is damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Puljic, this is --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Puljic, this photo comes from your book that is about damage post-Serb siege, so where do you see the damage?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over here on the minaret and you can see the top of the dome -- I mean it's not vertical and perhaps it had been shelled from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to show you --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Take a look. Can you see it here, the top of the minaret and the top of the dome that is slanted.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Puljic --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another thing, another thing, the Serb shelling did not stop when the left bank was liberated.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Right. And you indicated yesterday that you thought by February at least, February of 1993, it had stopped though?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always -- no --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well, we'll let the record speak for itself and let me ask you another question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, yesterday I asked the question or the day before yesterday, I can't remember. I asked you when the Serbs stopped shelling or shooting, it was a very specific question, and I believe you said a specific month. So what's your answer now? When did they stop? Did they stop at a particular date or did they keep shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serb shelling was there all the time; however, the intensity varied. The last Serb shell fell on Mostar on the day when it hit the Ero hotel where the European administration was and when in front of the Mostar cathedral three little girls were killed by a different Serb shell that evening. That is to say that the shelling went on all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What month and what year was it? Witness, the three little girls that were killed, when were they killed, what month and what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a date, the European administration had been in Mostar for another a year by then, I can't remember exactly; however, you can find this in documents. I think it was say in 1995. It was the summer of 1995 I think, but I know for sure that these were the last shells that came from the Serb positions, those that hit the hotel where the European administration was staying and then this shell that killed the three little girls in front of the cathedral.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 the Serbs are shelling. In 1993, in 1994, in 1995 as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Truth to tell, the intensity varied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Good. So you're confirming that there was shelling between 1992 and 1995, shelling from the Serbs, although you're saying that the intensity varied. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were periods when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good. Very well. Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, are you aware of what happened to this mosque later on?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a photo taken in May 1994, the first one. What's different about this photo than the one you previously saw?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The photograph was taken from a different angle, and the very top of the minaret is missing.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm going to show you the second photo. Can you also tell us what's different about that photo from the first one?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to know what it is you want to say. There -- the top of the minaret is missing, it fell off.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you know how that happened?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both you and I can only speculate. It could have been earthquake, and it could have just fallen off on its own, as often it used to happen; or it could have been damaged by the shell and then it was the result of shelling. It could have been knocked off by flying shell, and whatever I might say now comes into the sphere of speculation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, evidently the topic is mosques and the documents I showed to the witness. Let me draw your attention to an important matter. Document 2D 01421 that I showed to the witness which is the list of buildings made by the board of the Islamic community in Mostar, they say about Vucjakovic Mosque under 3 that it sustained major damage. The list was made in January 1993. In other words, the damage shown there was inflicted around that period. The witness did not see the list before. It was the Islamic community that produced the list, and I'm saying this merely so that you be mindful of what the Islamic community wrote about what the possibility of the shells falling on the mosque at the time in Mostar was and when.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was only now that I realized the source of the photographs. The source of the photographs is a new book called "Urbicide" made in Sarajevo a year or a year, or rather, a year and a half or two years after the other book titled "Urbicide." Can we please see the authors of this book and look at what their goals and intentions were. What I want to say is that the goal of this book was an honourable one, the intentions were honourable and honest, and the job was done correctly, professionally, responsibly, and objectively. I would like to have a look at the entire book called "Urbicide" and published in Sarajevo a year and a half or two years after my book before I can give any sort of an opinion on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with the institute of protection of cultural, historical, and natural heritage for the municipality of Mostar?
