utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that was an institution that was established in 1994 and it worked with UNESCO; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the name of the institution.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The institute of protection of cultural, historical, and natural heritage for the municipality of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Institute.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that I knew all the institutions in that field and this is the first time I hear of this term in the B/C/S "institut." I don't think that there is any such institution called that way in the B/C/S, and I don't think it had ever existed in Yugoslavia or in any of the republics. So I can claim that there is no "institut" for the protection of monuments in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, can you look at P 02264, it's the first binder. And this is a letter from Bishop Peric to General Petkovic and it's dated May 10th, 1993, and we'll just read the first paragraph. He says: "Dear General, it is my duty as a Bishop to express on behalf of the Catholic church in Mostar and on behalf of human and Catholic morality my deep disapproval of the destruction of the Muslim mosque on Balinovac, which occurred several minutes ago. The mosque is a place of worship where Islamic believers meet to play pray the honour and glory of good-Allah. The destruction of such building is a blow to the Holiest of Holies, all mighty God." Mr. Puljic, are you familiar with the Muslim mosque on Balinovac?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Baba Besirova Mosque, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that's the formal name of it; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Baba Besirova Mosque at Balinovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, and you'll agree with me that that mosque was destroyed on May 10th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a photo, this is P 09026, and we'll put them on the ELMO, the original, so they're easier to see. Is that the mosque on Balinovac?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'm going to show you the second photo which is an after shot. Is this what the area looked like after May 10th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Puljic, in Urbicide 2, you wrote an essay regarding bridges; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why Urbicide 2, Urbicide?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Sorry, 1992, "Urbicide."

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote an article in bridges in "Urbicide 1992."

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you had indicated that the Serbs blew up nine out of ten bridges; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: It is one bridge they didn't blow up was the Old Bridge; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm going to show you plate 65 and 66, these are in your book. Can you tell me if this is what the bridge looked like post-Serb siege?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, immediately after the Serb siege.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. And so look --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In other words, several days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And looking at the photo we see some damage on the -- from the photo, the upper left corner of the bridge. Do you see that damage?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we could show you the next plate, which is 66, that's just a better close-up shot of the damage; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. You testified I think it was the day before yesterday that you saw tank firing on the bridge on television; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And do you remember when that was, what month that was?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Is it possible that that could have been early November or late October of 1993?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember when it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. But would you agree with me that the bridge came down or the bridge collapsed in early or November 9th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And at that point the bridge had suffered a continual barrage of shelling from an HVO tank; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the TV broadcast said when it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, you testified that you were sorry that they fired on the bridge. Why are you sorry?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whenever a cultural monument is being destroyed I feel sorry. You were able to read that in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now we're going to show you P 007431 which is a video, and I think we can show it on the monitors.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you have this in front of you, Mr. Puljic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to start it over. It's in English, but it will be translated for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: "Christiane Amanpour: Up until about six months ago, the Muslims and the Croats were allied against the Serbs but perhaps Mostar is the best place to see how that alliance has crumbled. Indeed the Muslims, the Bosnian government, said that here the Croats have inflicted much more damage than the Serbs ever did. "The old town of Mostar had been devastated and the pride of this city the old bridge was finally destroyed by Croat tanks --"

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I just want you to focus on that part of the bridge when we saw that it was hit by a shell. Is it your memory that that was the state of the bridge during that period of time; do you remember seeing it like that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please be specific in your question. When? It is not specific enough for me to give you a specific answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: This would be the fall of 1993."

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is it about the fall of 1993 you're asking me.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did the bridge in 1993 look significantly different than it did post-Serb siege?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the fall of 1993 nobody was able to come close to this area. I saw the same thing you were able to see on the TV. I didn't see it at the time, so I can't compare the conditions when I didn't see anything other than the TV broadcast. The most appropriate thing to do here would be to give us the whole sequence of images of what the bridge looked like over those days after the initial damage because it had been constantly exposed to shelling. At a certain point one could still approach the bridge so it was covered with board work and tires. When the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats broke out, I couldn't come close to the bridge for the subsequent couple of years --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Puljic --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that's why I can't tell you what it looked like on the basis of what I was able to see because I wasn't able to see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, may I ask you another question --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now to compare the two images, well that's quite a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's go back to the original image and this is plate 66 in your book, so this is post-Serb siege, that's in front of you now. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you confirm for me that this is what the bridge -- the state of the bridge, this is what it looked like after the Serb siege?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're forcing me to compare what I was able to see with my own eyes with what I saw on the TV.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: No, no, no Mr. Puljic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Prosecution is not forcing you to do anything. The Prosecution is just showing you photographs and pictures and is asking you to give your opinion. Nobody is forcing you to do anything. Ms. West, we've talked about this bridge for -- at length for hundreds of hours, so please get to the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll move on from the bridge because I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, after the war between the Croats and the Muslims in 1993/1994, did your view or feelings towards the Muslim people change as a result of it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My feelings toward that particular people had always been the same. They're my neighbours with whom I -- or next to whom I live now and will be living for the rest of my life. There's a popular saying in Bosnia-Herzegovina that goes as follows: A neighbour is more important than a relative or a brother because he's right next to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That may be true, Mr. Puljic, but my question is: Did you emerge from the war with bad feelings towards them? Did you like them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I object to the form of the question. It's been asked and answered. If she wants to ask if he hates Muslims or Bosniaks, as they're called today, or if he has a grudge, she can just put the question to the gentleman. Let's not beat about the bush. If she wishes to ask these sorts of insulting questions, then she should just be as direct as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you might as well be as direct and frank.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Your Honour, I thought that was a direct question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The question was: Did you emerge with bad feelings towards them? Did you like them?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that over the past 50 years the Croatian people had been collectively accused, in this war and after this war, I did not accuse anyone collectively, not even the Muslim people. The Croatian people can perhaps accuse an individual and so can the Muslim people or the Serb people, but I think that we need to get out of this war. No one should bear a collective guilt the way the Croats bore a collective guilt for 50 years. At least we've learned something from history. So the Muslim people after this war do not have any collective guilt, I don't think that the Croatian people have any collective guilt, or the Serb people either. And that is precisely what you asked me, whether I'm blaming an entire people. You cannot blame an entire people.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Registrar, please, could we move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record we're now in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, can you go to the first binder, please, to P 10606. Now, after the -- Mr. Puljic, after the Washington Agreement in 1994 you also became -- or you became the deputy mayor of Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And during that time there were European Union negotiators in Mostar facilitating talks; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And their presence in Mostar was controversial among some; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe as far as some people are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that was because there were people who still wanted the city divided or at least controlled by Croats; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were emotions flowing throughout the city then; and a lot of time had to go by before people started crossing from one side to the other, on one day it would be two people, then three people, then five. There was enormous distrust between the two sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In the exhibit in front of you please turn to the article that's dated 2 August 1994. It says: "Tulsa World" on top, and I believe it's the third -- fourth page of this exhibit. Do you have that in front of you? This was an interview you gave in August of 1995 when you were the deputy mayor; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this interview.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll go through it. This was an interview with universal press -- well, with "Tulsa World" ultimately and it talks about Mostar and what had gone on and then it goes towards the bottom it talks about the neighbourhoods and at the very bottom of the English page it says: "The Croatian neighbourhoods are largely untouched. Kiosks are open and the people sit outside drinking coffee at cafes. Stolen Mercedes from Germany line the streets." And then there's actually a quote from you. Do you see the quote from you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot hear the speaker.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, do you see where we are?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. It's right about in the middle. It begins at the eighth paragraph down it begins with: "The Croatian neighbourhoods are largely untouched ..."

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And then the interviewer asks you a question and the question was: "What was the problem here we asked Boro Puljic, the deputy Croatian mayor that two peoples who had lived together for centuries are now divided by a river and by the silence that seems to hang over everything ." And your response was: "A clash of civilization, he immediately retorted. I wondered where he could have acquired such an Esoteric phrase and he said also said philosophically, ruminating on the revelations of the past that people had lived together previously because the communists had forced them to live together and sleep together." Now, sir, presumably you meant sleep together metaphorically, right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can state that I never expressed myself in those terms that they were sleeping together, what does this mean? Maybe the translation is poor or the journalist added something. What does that mean? I think that people sleep voluntarily and that they don't look at who is who then.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, this indicates that you said the communists had forced them, meaning the Croats and the Muslims, to live together. Do you see that part?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was written by the person who wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Correct. And this would suggest that at the time when you said it that you had a strong disdain for the Muslim people; would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see no disdain on the basis of this. Maybe you do.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's move on. By February 1998 you weren't the deputy mayor anymore, is that right, February 1998?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And when exactly did that happen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but to interrupt you, I believe that the phrase what you have quoted was that the communists forced them to live together and to sleep together, but later on the witness said that it was being said by the journalist, but I believe that it was not said by the journalist but by the witness according to you. I do not want to take in a way a stand as far as the authenticity of this article, that is another question. So I believe that it should be then made clear who was the author of that particular sentence which was quoted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Prandler.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let's move on to the -- I believe it's going to be the next article --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I believe -- excuse me. I believe based on your observations, Judge Prandler, you're asking the foundational question which should have been asked and I didn't want to intervene whether what is being reported here is what the gentleman stated. It's a yes or no. If yes, then you go on to the next one; if no, then perhaps: What did you say? Of course my learned colleague heard your observations and conveniently wants to move on. Now, it's called foundations, laying a foundation. Let's go step by step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: We speak about foundations many times, but it is frankly there is no need for any other foundation than the article which was quoted. The quote was being made by the Prosecution, by Ms. West. Afterwards that quotation was not rejected by the witness, and -- but later on he said that it was not being said by himself but by the journalist. My point was only to say and to ascertain if it was a kind of quotation from the journalist or it was a kind of statement submitted by the journalist. It is very simple. You do not know any more foundation. That was the article quoted and that's all. It is what I asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Judge Prandler, but he never accepted -- he was never even given an opportunity. The question was never posed: Did you say these things. He did indicate that this does not reflect what he indicated, but if you go back to the questioning -- the way -- the classical way of doing it is: I show you now this article. Did you give this interview? Yes or no. Okay then move on. Now it sates the following, did you say these things? Yes or no. If not, what did you say; if yes, let's talk about it. That's the step by step. But simply not giving him the opportunity to say does this accurately and correctly reflect what you said at the time, we cannot jump to the conclusion that he did not reject it, therefore it must be true that this is what he said. That's why I'm saying that we need to lay a foundation step by step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, did you say these words to the journalist? Did you actually say this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if someone forces you to sleep with someone then that is called rape. I never could have stated anything that stupid, that somebody was forcing me or us in the former Yugoslavia to rape each other. We slept together voluntarily. What the journalist wrote is stupid and I usually do not say things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'll move forward, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, if we can go to the next article and I believe it's going to be right behind this one, but the date is 21 February 1998 and it should say "BBC" on top. Now, you testified that by this time you were not deputy mayor anymore; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is an article about the construction of a Catholic church in Mostar and the article talks about it being controversial because the office of the High Representative was against it because they suggested it violated a Statute but the delegation from the Bishop conference went to the site and you were one of them. It says you and your brother were part of the delegation, including Mijo Brajkovic, he was the former mayor of Mostar; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a moment. It is true that I was at the construction site as the engineer overseeing the building of the church and that representatives of the church or the papal nuncio came. To my recollection, there were no partisan [as interpreted] representatives of the HDZ or Mijo Brajkovic or anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is the visit I have in mind, I don't recall the exact date. What I want to state is that I received the delegation as the overseeing engineer.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my recollection, neither the representatives of the HDZ nor Mijo Brajkovic and Mile Puljic were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, on line 22 the gentleman said party representatives not partisan representatives of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Puljic, let me direct your attention to part of this article, the bottom of the second paragraph it says: "The visit was attended by officials of the Croatian Democratic Union who have been replaced for their obstruction and extremism: Mijo Brajkovic, Boro Puljic, and Mile Puljic." Is Mile Puljic your brother?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The family name Puljic is very common in Herzegovina. If you take the directory, telephone directory, I'm sure you will find 2 to 3.000 telephone numbers to that name alone. Mile Puljic and I are not related.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. That was my question, you're not related. And so my next question is regarding the adjectives this writer uses, you didn't write this, they did, they said that you had been replaced for your obstruction and extremism. At that point you were not deputy mayor anymore; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not replaced at all. We were doing our job. After that the European administration in Mostar organized elections which elected a new Assembly, a new government, that replaced us, and we left, but we were not removed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So do you agree or not agree with the summation of this author that you were replaced because of -- or left because of obstruction and extremism?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Again, he indicated that he was voted out of office or chose not to run, one or the other -- but he says that he left. I mean, it's called democracy, people vote, you lose, you know, you're replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, if I can ask a more simple question that might bypass this. This author comes to a conclusion that you were extreme, and I gather from this sentence it meant extreme in your policies. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The author could not have been aware of my political views, and I disagree with the statement. I have never been an extremist.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So let's go to the same exhibit the very first article if you can back up a couple pages, the start of this exhibit, and it is a Dutch article by Dutch writer Bart Rijs, who covered the war for the Amsterdam newspaper. Do you have that article in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And here you were interviewed in November of 1995. The beginning of the interview is the writer just talking about the difficulties in Mostar, but then he says that under heavy international pressure the Croats and the Muslims signed a truce in the summer of 1994. The European Union got a mandate to govern Mostar for as long as two years. European officials, relief workers, and police officers put up at a hotel at the old front line and it was headed by a German EU mayor. The obligation was the city had to be reunited within two years. But if you go on in the article, he talks about there still being nonetheless two governments in Mostar and towards the end of it he interviews you and he talks about specifically the Croatian leadership and the western part of the city. This is towards the end. Do you see that? And it begins with: "The Croatian leadership and the western part of the city ..." And I'll read it: "The Croatian leadership in the western part of the city have systematically delayed and sabotaged the negotiations concerning the implementation of the EU mandate. Deputy mayor Borislav Puljic explains why. He draws a straight line across a blank sheet of paper and writes on the left: State number one, and on the right: State number two. He points at state number one and quotes: 'We want to live in a pure Croatian state, with the Croatian language and Croatian culture.' Then he draws a line -- excuse me, he draws a circle on the middle of the line: Mostar. 'If you unite the city, you'll have a third state, a multi-ethnic state where nobody is boss. That is a recipe for ... war.'" Mr. Puljic, do you remember making this drawing?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you remember saying this?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you deny this interview entirely?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the time-period when every day in my office or Mr. Brajkovic's office journalists would come and we gave interviews all the time. Can I kindly ask you to find in the archives of the European administration all my statements and all my activities during the work in the European Union and then you'll have a complete picture. To answer your question I should first read the entire article, since you're taking one sentence out of the context and want me to discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Puljic, my question is: Do you remember giving this interview?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This specific interview, no, but I'm telling you that I was giving interviews every day. I would give one to two interviews a day at the time. This is only one of a myriad of interviews given at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have to take a break. It will be a 15-minute break only. I think you still have some 15 minutes left at most, Mrs. West. Mr. Karnavas, for re-direct how much time will you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it all depends on what happens in the next 15 minutes, but I would say 15, 20 minutes tops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll have a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court's back in session. The registrar has made his computation, and you have 15 minutes left, Mrs. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, you testified that at the time in 1995 you gave numerous interviews; correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And that was interviews in your role as deputy mayor of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just ask, are we in private session or public? The screen here says private.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're still in private session, Mrs. West. Do you want us to go into open session?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We can go into open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since we live in a small town and there are attempts at discrediting me here, I would kindly ask you to move into closed session because of such attempts and all sorts of interpretation appearing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Prosecutor can ask for a private session when she believes that she's going to ask questions that deserve a private session and decide that we remain in open session when there's no need to move into private session. I don't know what questions she has in mind. If after the fact it is known that it should have been private session, you know, I can ask for a redaction. There is a 30-minute lag between what is being said now and what is being broadcast, so you're not at risk here. But I'm being very careful. Please continue, Mrs. West.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So it's your testimony that at the time you gave numerous interviews; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this was because you were the deputy mayor and so people came to interview regarding your political views on Mostar; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now -- but by 1998 you were not deputy mayor anymore. Did any international organization take any action against you or ban you from political activity?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. My activity was never political anyway. It always had to do with technical issues. I never occupied any of the political positions, and every post I held had to do with my profession and my professional qualifications.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, deputy mayor of Mostar is a political position, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you haven't completed your statement. Deputy mayor of Mostar for the field of urban planning and construction, so it wasn't a political position nor did it carry political weight. There were two deputy mayors, one for the field of urban planning and reconstruction and development of town and one for the remaining activities, affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: But the --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We coordinated all the activities that fell within our remit and were responsible to the mayor for those same issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. But notwithstanding, the interviews you gave in 1995 regarded your political views, as you indicated on line 8; right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was giving interviews every day and answering journalists' questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. So back to this Dutch interview, do you remember this particular interview?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. And even though you don't, is it possible you gave it because you gave so many at the time?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that I gave it since I was giving interviews almost every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And isn't it true, Mr. Puljic, that this statement: "'We want to live in a pure Croatian state, with the Croatian language and Croatian culture'" was your view in 1995?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not my view because when the war ended, Mr. Zubak called me to have a word with me. He said, or rather, he informed me of all the international negotiations and told me that peace had been introduced and new people had to be brought in who would be able to work along those lines. At the time, Mr. Brajkovic was appointed mayor and I was appointed deputy mayor and vice-president of the Croatian Defence Council for Mostar. We had the task of building a united town and ensuring that life -- of co-existence could take place there. How successful we were is something you can read in the reports of the European Union to who we were subjected at the time. Because while being municipal office holders, we were also holders of the European Union administration in Mostar and they supervised all the activities we undertook in that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, I see -- the question was: Was this your view in 1995. And you said: "This was not my view because ..." and you explained because at the time you were involved in these negotiations and you were the mayor and you had the task of building a united town. Sir, I don't believe that answers my question, that may have been your job, but my question is: Was this your view? Did you believe this? Did you believe that you wanted that people in Mostar should live in a pure Croatian state with the Croatian language and Croatian culture, regardless of what your job was?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My view then and now is that Mostar should be an indivisible united town in the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was my view then and is my view still. The indivisible united Bosnia-Herzegovina has to be organized in an equitable way guaranteeing equalities to all so that some peoples need not feel compelled to run out of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And in 1995 -- Mr. Puljic --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. In order to answer any one of these questions of yours, the entire article has to be looked at rather than taking everything out of context and looking at one sentence only. That is not enough for me to be able to answer such questions. My position then and now is the same: Mostar has to be a united, indivisible town.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you believe that the Croats should run it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That town should be governed by all those inhabiting it, namely, Croats, Muslims, and Serbs. Nobody has exclusive right over any particular town in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mrs. West. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Puljic, I just have very few questions. Now, in light of the -- I'm going to pick up where it was just ended. The insinuation is that you hate Muslims and that you want to have a Croat-only Mostar or Croat-only state within Bosnia-Herzegovina. First of all, you indicated to us that you are self-employed and you employ several engineers, architects, and what have you. Are any of your current employees Bosniaks or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I set up that company some ten or more years ago, and throughout the time the company employed Bosniaks and Serbs too, ever since its inception to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Were you forced to employ them or did you do this on your own?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I employed staff solely on the basis of knowledge and experience, and that is something that can be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, going back to this interview with the document which is P 10606, first I want to focus your attention to the fact that it's dated 10 November 1995, okay, and I want to -- I want you to think back to that period of time, November 10, 1995. Are you with me, Mr. Puljic? Mr. Puljic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I just have a couple of questions about this. First I want to focus your attention to 10 November 1995 because that's the period when this interview took place. Now, you've told us that you never drew a line and never drew this chart, but going back to that particular period -- sir, if you can just kindly focus on my questions as opposed to reading the document. Going back to that period of time, how many municipalities consisted of the Mostar municipality and what were the discussions going on at that particular time in light of the Dayton Peace Accords?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time there were three municipalities in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was there not --

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact date. In that period of time there existed three. There was, however, a stage when six Mostar municipalities were in the process of being established and I took part in those negotiations in Brussels.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, step by step, of the six municipalities how many of those were supposed to go to the Muslims and how many of those were supposed to go to the Croats? We're talking about this particular period of time.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PULJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of the municipalities were to end up belonging to any one side. They were supposed to be multi-ethnic. I took part in negotiations and we brought a document from Brussels that had been signed in Rome, whereby Mostar should be set up as a united town consisting of six municipalities that would not belong to any one people and a central zone. According to this document, all the legal structures of civilian authorities established hitherto were supposed to be invalidated. We based on this our first democratic elections after the war. When I say "we," I mean the European administration in Mostar and the Bosniak and Croats who worked within the European administration in Mostar. We implemented the Brussels agreement, or rather, it was the Rome agreement because it was signed in Rome. And on the basis of that agreement we carried out the first democratic elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Next, the one document that was shown to you by the Prosecutor which is P 0605, and that's the document from SIS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we're in open session. We would like Mr. Karnavas to tell us what is scheduled for next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have a witness, Your Honour, who we scheduled for three hours. We hope to do him in fewer than three, hopefully two. He will touch upon some of the same issues, although since they were covered extensively, probably not as extensively on direct examination, that is, the special-purpose council public enterprises. And then he will also discuss some areas into the -- related to his activities with the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and thereafter after the Washington and the Dayton Accords, his activities at the time. So that's -- we hope to have him finished on direct at least by Monday. We're very hopeful. And as we indicated, he's only for three hours, so most likely he's a three-day witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. I take the opportunity of having some minutes left to tell you that my fellow Judges and myself have looked at the schedule for all your upcoming witnesses, and we've noted recently that I believe you have some 13 witnesses left. When I sum up the time that would take about 63 hours but you only have 40 hours left, so maybe you have to reshuffle something. I mean, it's up to you of course, but please look into this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We have looked into it, Mr. President, and I can assure you that there are some -- there will be some changes which are not reflected in the calendar that you have. And in fact we hope to have -- reserve some time that we will use for direct with other witnesses. So we are not expecting to ask for any additional time, but we probably will go all the way up to the wire minus, say, five to six hours, maybe even more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's almost time to adjourn. As you know, next week we will be sitting Monday at 2.15 and then we'll be sitting in the afternoon for the rest of the week. Thank you. That's all I had to say. Mr. Scott would like to add something? We haven't heard you for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sure everyone's grateful for that, Your Honour. No, Your Honour, thank you very much. I think we should be in good shape for next week. Thank you. I wish everyone a good weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. See you next week then.
